clinicalPearls: Caused by chronic infection with human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, and endemic in south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of Africa, and South America
Recognised as four clinical variants (acute, lymphomatous, chronic, and smouldering) with widely differing behaviour and treatment
Characteristic features include lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, hypercalcaemia with lytic bone lesions, and a raised lactate dehydrogenase
The circulating malignant cells are mature CD4-positive T-cells expressing CD25, classically with multilobated 'flower cell' nuclei
Profound immunosuppression predisposes to opportunistic infections, notably Strongyloides hyperinfection and Pneumocystis pneumonia
Diagnosis rests on HTLV-1 seropositivity together with a clonal CD4/CD25-positive T-cell population and clonal integration of the provirus
Aggressive variants are treated with combination chemotherapy or antiviral-based approaches, with allogeneic transplantation and anti-CCR4 antibody therapy in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma is a mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm driven by long-term infection with human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, usually acquired in infancy through breastfeeding or later through blood or sexual transmission. The viral regulatory proteins, particularly Tax and HBZ, dysregulate host cell proliferation, survival, and genomic stability, and after a long latency a clone of infected T-cells transforms. The neoplastic cells frequently have a regulatory T-cell-like phenotype, contributing to immunosuppression, and secrete factors that stimulate osteoclasts, producing the characteristic hypercalcaemia and lytic bone disease. Only a small proportion of infected individuals develop overt disease.
additionalDifferentials: Sezary syndrome and other cutaneous T-cell lymphomas
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
Other mature T-cell leukaemias such as T-prolymphocytic leukaemia
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy from other tumours
additionalInvestigations: HTLV-1 serology and confirmatory testing with proviral load
Peripheral blood film for flower cells and flow cytometry (CD4, CD25)
Demonstration of clonal HTLV-1 proviral integration or T-cell clonality
Serum calcium, lactate dehydrogenase, and skeletal assessment for lytic lesions
Cross-sectional imaging and bone marrow examination for staging and subtyping
Screening for Strongyloides and other opportunistic infections before immunosuppressive therapy
redFlags: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with renal impairment or altered consciousness
Opportunistic infection such as Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome
Rapid progression of the acute or lymphomatous variant with high tumour burden
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on subtype: the acute and lymphomatous variants are aggressive with poor survival, whereas chronic and smouldering forms are more indolent though still capable of transformation, and hypercalcaemia and high tumour burden portend worse outcomes.
pitfalls: Failing to test for HTLV-1 in patients from endemic regions with a T-cell malignancy
Not screening for and treating Strongyloides before immunosuppression, risking fatal hyperinfection
Missing hypercalcaemia as a presenting emergency
Misclassifying the clinical variant and therefore mismatching treatment intensity
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
